title: A survey on machine learning methods for churn prediction
venue: International Journal of Data Science and Analytics
harvard_reference: Geiler, L., Affeldt, S. and Nadif, M. (2022) 'A survey on machine learning methods for churn prediction', International Journal of Data Science and Analytics, 14(3), pp. 217-242. doi:10.1007/s41060-022-00312-5.
abstract_summary: A technical survey plus benchmark of supervised and semi-supervised churn-prediction methods. The authors evaluate eleven learning methods (k-NN, Gaussian Naive Bayes, logistic regression, linear and RBF SVM, decision tree, random forest, XGBoost, a feed-forward neural network, GEV-NN, plus the anomaly-detection methods iForest and DevNet) combined with seven sampling strategies (none, SMOTE, ADASYN, NCR, Tomek Links, SMOTE+random undersampling, SMOTE+Tomek, SMOTE+NCR) on sixteen public 'churn-like' datasets, including the IBM Telco churn set (TelC), using stratified 5-fold cross-validation and AUC with default hyperparameters. Results are compared with the Nemenyi post-hoc test / critical-difference diagrams and Correspondence Analysis. Across all datasets and sampling strategies the top individual methods are LR, RF, XGBoost and NN (mean ranks 2.61, 3.21, 3.33, 3.66); sampling produces only small AUC variations and generally degrades RF. The paper's practical recommendation is a probability-averaging ensemble of LR, XGBoost and RF with no sampling (median AUC 0.8577), which nearly matches the best single pipeline on almost every dataset.

claims_supported.claim: A survey and benchmark of churn-prediction methods across many datasets finds that ensemble tree methods and logistic regression are among the strongest, and that handling class imbalance is a central design decision.
claims_supported.where: Abstract: 'we study the behavior of eleven supervised and semi-supervised learning methods and seven sampling approaches on sixteen diverse and publicly available churn-like datasets'. Section 6.2.1: 'The top approaches over all datasets and sampling strategies are LR, RF, XGBoost and NN, with a mean rank of 2.61, 3.21, 3.33 and 3.66 respectively'; Section 6.2.3: 'in practice, we recommend the use of the ensemble LR|XGBoost|RF with no sampling for analyzing novel churn-like datasets'. On imbalance: Abstract: 'Choosing a priori the most appropriate sampling method as well as the most suitable classification model is not trivial, as it strongly depends on the data intrinsic characteristics'; Section 3: 'Customer defection is an infrequent event that is inevitably associated with a class imbalance hassle that impedes the quality of customer churn prediction'. The whole benchmark pipeline (Fig. 2) is organised around the sampling-method x classifier choice, so imbalance handling is treated as a core design axis. CAVEAT for the report: the paper's empirical finding is that resampling matters little for AUC ('only small AUC variations over sampling strategies'; 'sampling methods generally degrade AUC for RF'; 'the sampling strategies have a weak effect on the machine learning approaches ranking') and its recommended pipeline uses NO sampling. Do not cite this paper as evidence that SMOTE/resampling improves churn models; cite it as evidence that the choice must be made deliberately and evaluated, and that tree ensembles are largely robust to it.

claims_supported.claim: Deep learning did not clearly outperform gradient boosting on typical churn datasets in their benchmark.
claims_supported.where: The paper makes no statement comparing 'deep learning' as a family against gradient boosting, and the tables only partly support the claim. Evidence consistent with it: the plain feed-forward NN ranks below LR, RF and XGBoost overall (mean rank 3.66 vs 2.61/3.21/3.33) and has median AUC 0.7700 vs XGBoost 0.8104 without sampling (Table 2); DevNet (median AUC 0.7353, rank 6.31) is clearly worse; the recommended ensemble LR|XGBoost|RF omits the neural network; Nemenyi CD diagrams connect the top approaches, i.e. no method is statistically separable from the top group. Evidence AGAINST the claim as worded: GEV-NN (a deep network designed for imbalanced data) obtains the best mean rank (2.88) and the highest median AUC (0.8542) of all twelve methods in the no-sampling comparison, ahead of XGBoost (rank 4.44, AUC 0.8104), and is the best single pipeline for two datasets in Table 8. Also, XGBoost is not the strongest single model here (LR and RF rank above it), and all models use default hyperparameters. A defensible rewording: 'In Geiler et al.'s (2022) benchmark, a default feed-forward neural network ranked below logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost, and their recommended ensemble combines LR, XGBoost and RF without a neural component; only the imbalance-specific GEV-NN was competitive with the tree ensembles, and no method was statistically separable from the top group.'
